summary:
Mars Walk is a browser-based 3D survival simulator of Gale Crater on Mars, built entirely from real NASA data. You explore on foot as an astronaut or drive the Curiosity rover at its real top speed of about 4 cm/s. The terrain comes from HiRISE stereo elevation data, CTX images and MOLA. Curiosity's route comes from NASA MMGIS, and the clock runs on true Mars time (Mars24). Weather, dust and radiation follow measurements from Curiosity's REMS, Mastcam and RAD instruments. Oxygen and suit power drain at rates taken from NASA spacesuit data. You can collect 24 real rock samples at the spots where Curiosity studied them, each with its NASA photo.

It answers the challenge with a layered, integrated map of Gale Crater that combines data from MRO, Mars Global Surveyor and Curiosity. A future explorer can use it to plan a Marswalk: where to go, what conditions to expect and how long their oxygen and power will last.

This matters because Mars data usually stays in archives and scientific papers. Mars Walk turns it into an experience anyone can explore in a web browser, in English or Turkish, with every number linked to its source.
details:
What it does

Mars Walk is a 3D survival simulator of Gale Crater that runs in any modern web browser, with nothing to install. You start next to NASA's Curiosity rover at its real, current position, on the real date and time on Mars. From there you explore on foot as an astronaut or drive Curiosity yourself. An elevation map shows the crater, Mount Sharp and Curiosity's actual route, and you can jump to any point on it.

How it works

  • Terrain: HiRISE stereo elevation on a 2 m grid near the player, then a 12 m ring, then a MOLA–HRSC model out to 131 km. A continuous level-of-detail technique (CDLOD) blends them smoothly.
  • Time: the Mars24 algorithm turns the Earth date into the sol, local Mars time, season and sun position. There are three scenarios: today, landing day (6 August 2012) and the 2018 global dust storm, replayed from 104 real measurements.
  • Environment: temperature, pressure, wind, dust and visibility follow Curiosity's REMS and Mastcam records by season, hour and elevation. The radiation dose follows RAD measurements, including shielding from air pressure and terrain.
  • Survival: oxygen and suit battery drain at NASA spacesuit rates that change when you rest, walk or run. When either runs out, the spacewalk ends.
  • Rover: Curiosity moves at its real top speed of about 4 cm/s, stops on slopes steeper than 30° and uses a model of its real nuclear power source (RTG) and battery. A time-warp key makes long drives possible.
  • Science: 24 real rock targets sit at Curiosity's position on the sol it studied them, at real size, textured with NASA photos and showing drill holes and brush marks.

Benefits and intended impact

Mars data usually lives in archives and scientific papers. Mars Walk turns it into something students and the public can experience: how big Gale Crater is, how slow a rover really is, how thin the air is and how long a person could last outside. It is free and bilingual (English and Turkish), and every number links to its source, so teachers can use it in class and players can check the science themselves. We hope it inspires students, especially in Türkiye, to work with real space data.

Tools, languages, hardware and software

JavaScript, HTML, CSS and GLSL shaders with three.js (WebGL2). A Python data pipeline (GDAL, rasterio, NumPy, Pillow) reads only the needed regions of multi-gigabyte USGS files through HTTP range requests. FFmpeg for the video, Vercel for hosting, and Claude (Anthropic) as an AI coding assistant. Hardware: a regular laptop; the app runs on any computer with a WebGL2 browser.

What makes it creative

Instead of a fictional Mars, the project follows a strict "no invented numbers" rule. The clock is tied to the real calendar, so every visit is a different Martian day. Rock samples appear where Curiosity studied them, and you can relive the 2018 dust storm that ended the Opportunity rover's mission.

Factors we considered

  • Accuracy versus playability: real speeds and consumption rates, plus a time warp that is capped so the simulation stays stable.
  • Honesty: elements that do not come from data, such as an astronaut walking beside Curiosity, are labeled in the game.
  • Performance: about 36 MB of data and 60 fps on a regular laptop in our tests.
  • Accessibility: browser-based, no account needed, two languages.
  • Licensing: NASA public-domain data and open-source libraries, all credited in the in-game Sources panel.
